source: Editorial profiles written for Plantivorous. Nomenclatural facts cross-checked against the ICPS Carnivorous Plant Names Resource.

genera.nativeRange: Scattered freshwater wetlands across Europe, Asia, Africa and Australia
genera.description: Aldrovanda vesiculosa is a rootless, free-floating aquatic sundew whose whorls of leaves look like the paddles of a waterwheel. Each leaf ends in a small snap trap, one of the fastest active traps in the plant kingdom. The plant spends summer at the water surface and survives winter as a dormant turion at the bottom of the pond.
genera.identification: Look for floating whorls of six to eight leaves, each tipped with a translucent, hinged trap and fine trigger hairs. The traps are only a few millimetres long.
genera.ecology: It grows in shallow, acidic, nutrient-poor water and is sensitive to pollution, drainage and eutrophication. Wild populations are widely scattered and declining, making it a flagship for wetland conservation.

care.overview: A specialist aquarium and pond plant. It needs soft, acidic water, strong light and a cool winter rest. It is not a beginner plant.
care.light: Full sun to very bright light; outdoors in a shallow tub is best.
care.water: Soft, acidic, mineral-free water. Keep the water warm in summer and cool in winter; avoid hard tap water entirely.
care.soil: No soil. Float the plants in water; add a little live sphagnum or a mesh anchor if needed.
care.temperature: Summer 20–30°C; winter 4–10°C for turion formation and dormancy.
care.dormancy: Forms turions in autumn. Keep turions cool and submerged; restart in spring.
care.feeding: Feed tiny aquatic invertebrates or a very dilute aquarium invertebrate food. Do not overfeed.
care.propagation: Division of floating stems in summer; turions in winter.
care.problems: Hard water, algae, overheating, snails and fish. Wild-collected plants are best avoided.

genera.nativeRange: Australia and New Guinea, with the greatest diversity in the tropical north and south-west
genera.description: Byblis leaves are covered with glandular hairs that glitter in the sun and produce a rainbow-like sheen. Insects stick to the mucilage and are digested by the plant. The genus includes small annuals and taller, shrubby perennials, and is unrelated to the superficially similar sundews.
genera.identification: Leaves are narrow and grass-like, with sticky glands on the upper surface and a simple or branched stem. Flowers are usually mauve to purple.
genera.ecology: Most species grow in sandy, seasonally wet heathland. Annuals complete their life cycle in the wet season and survive the dry season as seed; perennials develop woody stems and may die back to a rootstock.

care.overview: Bright light, warm temperatures and constantly damp, sandy, nutrient-poor soil. Annuals are best raised from seed each season.
care.light: Full sun to very bright light.
care.water: Stand in 1–3 cm of mineral-free water during growth. Never let the mix dry out while plants are growing.
care.soil: Peat : sand 1:1, or a very sandy peat mix. Keep it open and low in nutrients.
care.dormancy: Annuals die after seeding; perennials may die back in the dry season.
care.feeding: They catch their own insects. Do not fertilise.
care.propagation: Seed, sown on the surface of wet sandy peat. Perennials can be divided.
care.problems: Damping-off, root disturbance, hard water and aphids.

annual.label: Annual
annual.notes: Sow fresh seed in warm, bright conditions and keep the surface wet. Plants self-seed readily when happy.

perennial.label: Perennial
perennial.notes: Grow in deep pots so the rootstock has room. Reduce water during the dry-season rest.

genera.nativeRange: A small corner of the south-west Western Australian coast near Albany
genera.description: Cephalotus follicularis is the only species in its family and one of the most distinctive pitcher plants. It produces a basal rosette of ordinary leaves and ribbed, tooth-rimmed pitchers with a lid. The pitchers are small but remarkably efficient, and the plant's strange, almost reptilian look has made it a collector's favourite.
genera.identification: Squat pitchers with a toothed peristome and a domed lid; mature plants form tight clumps. The pitcher body is often mottled green, red and purple.
genera.ecology: It grows in sandy, peaty swamps and seepages in a Mediterranean climate, with wet winters and drier summers. Habitat loss and illegal collection are significant threats.

care.overview: A compact, slow-growing plant for a cool, bright position. It resents hot roots, hard water and being kept bone dry.
care.light: Bright light with some direct sun; avoid scorching summer heat.
care.water: Tray water with mineral-free water. Keep the mix moist year-round, slightly drier in summer.
care.soil: Peat : sand : perlite 2:1:1. A top dressing of live sphagnum helps keep humidity even.
care.temperature: Cool to intermediate: 10–25°C. Protect from prolonged heat above 30°C.
care.dormancy: No true dormancy. Growth slows in hot, dry summers; do not let the roots desiccate.
care.feeding: Feed only occasionally with small insects; the pitchers catch their own food outdoors.
care.propagation: Leaf cuttings, division, root cuttings and seed. Be patient: seedlings are slow.
care.problems: Root rot from stale, waterlogged soil, hard water, mealybugs and scale.

genera.nativeRange: South America, mainly Brazil and neighbouring countries
genera.description: Craniolaria is a small genus of sticky-leaved annuals in the Martyniaceae. The leaves and stems are covered with glandular hairs that trap small insects, but the plants are not as strongly carnivorous as Drosera or Pinguicula. They are grown mostly as curiosities and for their unusual seed pods.
genera.identification: Soft, hairy annual with opposite leaves and tubular flowers; the fruit develops a long, woody beak.
genera.ecology: Seasonally dry, open habitats. The sticky glands are thought to deter herbivores as well as capture small insects.

care.overview: An easy warm-season annual from seed. Treat it as a drought-tolerant curiosity rather than a high-maintenance carnivore.
care.water: Moderate; let the surface dry between waterings. Avoid waterlogging.
care.soil: Free-draining sandy loam or a cactus-style mix.
care.temperature: Warm; sow after the last frost.
care.dormancy: Annual; dies after setting seed.
care.feeding: No feeding required.
care.propagation: Seed sown directly in warm conditions.
care.problems: Aphids, spider mites and damping-off in cool, wet soil.

genera.nativeRange: Mountain seeps and serpentine wetlands of northern California and south-western Oregon
genera.description: Darlingtonia californica is instantly recognisable: its tubular leaves arch over into a hooded head with a forked appendage that looks like a snake's tongue. Insects enter through openings under the hood and are guided down into the pitcher. The plant is the only species in its genus and is prized by collectors for its sculptural form.
genera.identification: Hooded, cobra-like pitchers with a forked 'tongue' and a small opening beneath the hood. Pitchers arise from a creeping rhizome.
genera.ecology: It grows in cold, flowing seeps and fens, often on serpentine soil. It needs cool roots and clean water; wild populations are threatened by water extraction, development and poaching.

care.overview: The key is cool, moving water and cool roots. This is not a plant for a hot windowsill.
care.light: Full sun to bright light; in hot climates provide afternoon shade.
care.water: Constant flow of cool, mineral-free water is ideal. Keep the mix wet and the roots below 25°C.
care.soil: Peat : perlite : sand 2:1:1, with a top dressing of live sphagnum.
care.dormancy: Winter dormancy is required. Keep cool and moist, not frozen solid.
care.feeding: Outdoor plants catch their own insects. Do not fertilise.
care.propagation: Division of rhizomes in late winter; seed (slow and variable).
care.problems: Root rot in stagnant water, heat stress, aphids and scale.

genera.nativeRange: A small area of coastal North and South Carolina, USA
genera.description: Dionaea muscipula is the most famous carnivorous plant in the world. Each leaf ends in two hinged lobes armed with trigger hairs and marginal teeth; two touches within about twenty seconds can snap the trap shut. The genus is monotypic, but centuries of cultivation have produced an extraordinary range of cultivars.
genera.identification: Paired, jaw-like lobes with marginal teeth and three trigger hairs on each lobe. Traps are held on short, broad petioles in a rosette.
genera.ecology: It grows in wet, acidic, nutrient-poor pine savannas and bogs that depend on frequent fire. Wild populations are threatened by habitat loss and poaching; the species is protected in the wild.

care.overview: A rewarding beginner plant if it gets full sun, clean water and a cool winter dormancy. The most common mistake is keeping it warm and wet indoors all winter.
care.light: Full sun outdoors; a very bright, sunny windowsill indoors.
care.water: Stand in 2–5 cm of mineral-free water during growth. Use rainwater, distilled or reverse-osmosis water.
care.soil: Peat : perlite or silica sand 1:1. Never use ordinary potting soil or fertiliser.
care.dormancy: Needs a cool winter rest of 8–12 weeks. Reduce water but do not let the mix dry completely.
care.feeding: Feed live insects occasionally, or let the plant catch its own. Never feed meat or fertiliser.
care.propagation: Division in late winter, leaf cuttings, flower-stalk cuttings and seed.
care.problems: Root rot, sunburn after a sudden move, aphids, spider mites and scale.

genera.nativeRange: Tropical West and Central Africa
genera.description: Dioncophyllum thollonii is a tropical liana in the Dioncophyllaceae, a family that also contains the famous Triphyophyllum. Its leaves bear glandular structures and the plant has been discussed as a possible proto-carnivore, but it is not a practical cultivated carnivore. It is included here for completeness of the ICPS register.
genera.identification: A woody liana with alternate leaves and hooked climbing structures; the glandular leaf surfaces are subtle.
genera.ecology: Rainforest liana of tropical Africa. Its carnivorous status is debated and difficult to study in the field.

care.overview: Not recommended for cultivation. It requires tropical rainforest conditions and a large climbing structure, and is essentially a botanical-garden curiosity.
care.water: High humidity and evenly moist, free-draining soil.
care.soil: Loose, humus-rich tropical mix.
care.dormancy: None.
care.feeding: Not applicable in cultivation.
care.propagation: Seed or stem cuttings, with difficulty.
care.problems: Not a houseplant; leave wild plants undisturbed.

genera.nativeRange: Every continent except Antarctica, with centres of diversity in Australia, South Africa and South America
genera.description: Drosera is the largest genus of carnivorous plants, with more than 190 accepted species. Each leaf is covered with stalked glands that secrete a glistening drop of mucilage; insects stick, and the leaf may slowly curl around the prey. Sundews range from tiny pygmy rosettes to the giant Drosera regia, and from tropical epiphytes to winter-growing tuberous species.
genera.identification: Leaves with visible stalked glands and clear mucilage droplets. Growth forms include rosettes, upright stems, climbing stems, tubers and pygmy rosettes.
genera.ecology: Sundews occupy nutrient-poor wetlands, seepages, heathlands and inselbergs. Many are fire-adapted, and several groups have precise seasonal dormancy. Some species are among the most threatened plants in their habitats.

care.overview: Sundews want bright light, mineral-free water and a nutrient-poor acidic mix. The right care depends strongly on the species group: temperate, subtropical, Cape winter-growing, pygmy, tuberous, petiolaris or annual.
care.light: Full sun to very bright light. Indoors, use a powerful grow light.
care.water: Tray water with rainwater, distilled or reverse-osmosis water. Keep the mix wet during growth.
care.soil: Peat : perlite or silica sand 1:1. Some groups prefer sandier or more organic mixes.
care.temperature: Depends on the group. Temperate species need cool winters; tropical species need warmth year-round.
care.dormancy: Many species have a dry, cool or cold dormant season. Match the group.
care.feeding: Let them catch their own insects. A very occasional tiny insect is enough; never fertilise the soil.
care.propagation: Seed, leaf cuttings, root cuttings and division, depending on the group.
care.problems: Hard water, root rot, aphids, thrips, spider mites, mildew and drying out.

temperate.label: Temperate
temperate.water: Stand in 2–5 cm of mineral-free water during growth.
temperate.temperature: Cool to mild; winter cold is required.
temperate.dormancy: Cold winter dormancy. Many die back to resting buds.
temperate.notes: Hardy outdoor bog plants for temperate climates. Keep the bog wet and open to the sun.

subtropical.label: Subtropical / warm-temperate
subtropical.temperature: Warm to mild; protect from hard frost.
subtropical.dormancy: Growth slows in winter; no hard dormancy.
subtropical.notes: The forgiving group that includes Drosera capensis and D. aliciae. Good beginner sundews.

cape.label: Cape winter-growing
cape.water: Wet during winter growth; much drier in summer dormancy.
cape.temperature: Cool, Mediterranean; protect from summer heat.
cape.notes: These South African species grow in winter rain and rest dry in summer. Do not keep them wet year-round.

pygmy.label: Pygmy sundew
pygmy.light: Full sun; strong light keeps the rosettes compact and colourful.
pygmy.water: Wet during winter growth; drier in summer.
pygmy.soil: Very sandy peat, low in nutrients.
pygmy.temperature: Cool to mild; avoid hot, humid nights.
pygmy.dormancy: Dry summer dormancy; many form gemmae.
pygmy.notes: Pygmy sundews are small, jewel-like Australian species. Gemmae are the easiest way to propagate them.

tuberous.label: Tuberous
tuberous.water: Wet during winter growth; completely dry during summer dormancy.
tuberous.soil: Deep, very sandy peat with sharp drainage.
tuberous.notes: Use deep pots so the tuber has room. Keep dry in summer and resume watering when new growth appears.

petiolaris.label: Petiolaris complex
petiolaris.water: Wet during the wet season; drier during the dry-season dormancy.
petiolaris.dormancy: Dry-season dormancy; plants may die back to a hairy resting bud.
petiolaris.notes: A challenging group from tropical northern Australia. They need heat, light and a pronounced dry rest.

annual.label: Annual
annual.notes: Sow fresh seed and let the colony self-seed. A fast, fun group.

genera.nativeRange: South-western Iberia and north-western Morocco
genera.description: Drosophyllum lusitanicum is a shrubby, woody-based carnivore from the dry Mediterranean fringe. Its long, narrow leaves are covered with sticky glands and curl slightly at the tips. Unlike most carnivores it grows in relatively dry, alkaline or neutral soils, and it is notoriously difficult to transplant.
genera.identification: A woody shrub with long, narrow, dewy leaves and yellow flowers. The leaves are not arranged in a rosette and the plant can reach 1 m across.
genera.ecology: It grows in open, dry, sunny scrub on sandy or stony soils, often after fire. It is threatened by development, afforestation and collection.

care.overview: Grow it in a deep, well-drained pot, keep the roots dry-ish, and never disturb the roots. This is a plant for experienced growers.
care.water: Water deeply but infrequently, then let the mix dry. Avoid tray water and humid, stagnant air.
care.soil: A very free-draining mineral mix: coarse sand, perlite, pumice and a little peat or leaf mould.
care.temperature: Mediterranean: warm, dry summers and cool, damp winters. Protect from frost.
care.dormancy: No true dormancy, but growth slows in the hottest part of summer.
care.feeding: Self-catches; do not feed.
care.propagation: Seed, sown in deep pots. Avoid transplanting; sow in the final container.
care.problems: Root disturbance, rot, spider mites and scale.

genera.nativeRange: Tropical Africa, Madagascar and South America, with a centre of diversity in Brazil
genera.description: Genlisea is a genus of small rosette plants related to Utricularia. Below ground it produces remarkable spiral, lobster-pot traps that guide tiny invertebrates into a digestive chamber. The traps are among the most complex in the plant kingdom. Many species have yellow or violet flowers on tall scapes.
genera.identification: Small rosettes of spoon-shaped leaves with tall flower scapes. The real traps are underground and rarely seen; repotting reveals the corkscrew structures.
genera.ecology: They grow in wet, sandy, nutrient-poor soils and seepages, often in seasonal savanna or campos rupestres. Some species are aquatic or semi-aquatic.

care.overview: Treat Genlisea like a small terrestrial Utricularia: wet, bright and nutrient-poor. The underground traps need a loose, airy mix.
care.water: Keep the mix very wet; tray water is fine.
care.soil: Peat : sand : perlite 1:1:1, with live sphagnum on the surface.
care.temperature: Warm to intermediate; protect from frost.
care.dormancy: Some species die back to a resting bud in the dry season.
care.feeding: Do not feed; the traps capture microfauna.
care.propagation: Leaf cuttings, division, seed.
care.problems: Algae, aphids, drying out, root rot in stale water.

genera.nativeRange: Tropical West Africa
genera.description: Habropetalum dawei is a rare tropical liana in the Dioncophyllaceae. Like its relatives, it has glandular leaves and has been discussed as a possible proto-carnivore. It is not cultivated as a carnivorous plant and is included primarily for completeness of the ICPS register.
genera.identification: Woody liana with alternate leaves and hooked climbing structures; flowers are large and showy.
genera.ecology: Tropical forest liana, poorly known. Its carnivorous status is uncertain.

care.overview: Not recommended for cultivation; it needs tropical forest conditions and a large climbing structure.
care.water: High humidity and evenly moist, free-draining soil.
care.soil: Humus-rich tropical mix.
care.dormancy: None.
care.feeding: Not applicable.
care.propagation: Seed or cuttings, with difficulty.
care.problems: Not a houseplant; leave wild plants undisturbed.

genera.nativeRange: Tepuis of the Guiana Highlands in Venezuela, Guyana and Brazil
genera.description: Heliamphora species grow on the remote, rain-lashed summits of the Guiana Highlands. Their pitchers are formed from rolled leaves with a small, often red-veined lid and a nectar-secreting rim. They are among the most distinctive pitcher plants and can form dense, sculptural clumps.
genera.identification: Tall, slender or squat pitchers with a small lid, often red-veined, emerging from a rhizome. Flowers are white to pink on tall scapes.
genera.ecology: They grow in wet, peaty, nutrient-poor soils on tepui summits and slopes, often in full sun and constant wind. Endemism is high and many species have tiny ranges.

care.overview: A highland plant: strong light, high humidity, cool nights and constantly moist, airy soil. Warm nights are the main killer.
care.light: Very bright light; full sun is often tolerated if humidity is high.
care.water: Mineral-free water, kept cool. Top-water frequently and keep the mix wet.
care.soil: Peat : perlite : live sphagnum 1:1:1, in a tall pot.
care.temperature: Day 18–26°C; night 8–16°C. A night drop is essential.
care.dormancy: No true dormancy, though growth slows in winter.
care.feeding: Small insects in the pitchers; do not fertilise.
care.propagation: Division of rhizomes, seed.
care.problems: Heat stress, root rot, hard water, aphids and scale.

genera.nativeRange: South America, naturalised in warm regions elsewhere
genera.description: Ibicella lutea is a sprawling annual with soft, sticky, strongly scented leaves and yellow flowers. It traps small insects on glandular hairs but is only weakly carnivorous. The common name comes from the large, woody, claw-like seed pods.
genera.identification: Large, opposite, sticky leaves; yellow tubular flowers; distinctive hooked seed capsules.
genera.ecology: A weed of disturbed, warm, often dry ground. It is fast-growing and self-seeds readily.

care.overview: An easy annual curiosity. Grow it in full sun and poor, well-drained soil; do not baby it.
care.water: Moderate; let the surface dry between waterings.
care.soil: Poor, sandy or stony soil with sharp drainage.
care.dormancy: Annual; dies after seeding.
care.feeding: No feeding needed.
care.propagation: Seed. Soak the hard seed coat first.
care.problems: Aphids, spider mites, powdery mildew.

genera.nativeRange: Mexico and Central America; naturalised in the tropics
genera.description: Martynia annua is a sticky, glandular annual in the Martyniaceae. It catches small insects on its leaves and stems but is not a true carnivore in the strict sense. The plant is grown mainly for its dramatic, hooked seed pods.
genera.identification: Coarse annual with opposite, sticky-hairy leaves, pinkish tubular flowers and large wooden seed pods with two curved claws.
genera.ecology: Disturbed ground, roadsides and dry scrub in the tropics and subtropics.

care.overview: Easy from seed in warm, sunny conditions. Treat it as a curiosity annual.
care.water: Moderate; well-drained soil.
care.soil: Poor, sandy loam.
care.dormancy: Annual.
care.feeding: No feeding.
care.propagation: Seed.
care.problems: Aphids and spider mites.

genera.nativeRange: Old World tropics: South-East Asia, Madagascar, Seychelles, New Guinea, northern Australia and islands of the Indian and Pacific Oceans
genera.description: Nepenthes is the great genus of tropical pitcher plants, with more than 120 accepted species and a bewildering array of natural hybrids. The pitchers are modified leaf tips, often brightly coloured, with a slippery peristome and a lid. They range from tiny ground pitchers to the enormous, rat-dissolving pitchers of Nepenthes rajah.
genera.identification: Pitchers with a distinct peristome and lid, usually produced at the end of a tendril. Lower and upper pitchers often look completely different.
genera.ecology: They grow from sea-level swamps to cloud-forest summits, on ultramafic soils, sandstone cliffs and epiphytically in mossy forest. Many have tiny ranges and are threatened by habitat loss and collection.

care.overview: Nepenthes care depends on altitude. Lowland species want warmth and humidity; highland species want a cool night drop. Intermediate forms are the most forgiving.
care.light: Bright, filtered light. Avoid harsh midday sun on young plants.
care.water: Keep the mix evenly moist but airy. Use mineral-free water; never let the pot sit in stagnant water.
care.soil: Sphagnum moss, perlite and bark, or a loose peat : perlite : bark mix.
care.temperature: Depends on the group; see the specific care group.
care.dormancy: No dormancy. Growth slows in cool or very dry conditions.
care.feeding: Feed small insects into the pitchers or use a very dilute orchid fertiliser occasionally. Do not overfeed.
care.propagation: Stem cuttings, basal shoots, tissue culture and seed.
care.problems: Root rot, crown rot, thrips, mealybugs, scale, sudden humidity drops.

lowland.label: Lowland
lowland.notes: Warm, humid and steady. Good for beginners in tropical climates; challenging in cool houses.

highland.label: Highland
highland.notes: The night drop is essential. Use a cool greenhouse, cellar or terrarium with night cooling.

intermediate.label: Intermediate
intermediate.notes: The most adaptable group. Many popular hybrids thrive here.

genera.nativeRange: Northern Hemisphere, with centres of diversity in Mexico and the Mediterranean; also tropical Americas
genera.description: Pinguicula leaves are flat, usually pale green rosettes covered with microscopic sticky glands. Small insects stick to the leaf and are digested in a shallow depression. The genus includes temperate bog species, tropical epiphytes and the remarkable Mexican 'butterworts' that form succulent winter rosettes.
genera.identification: Flat, fleshy rosettes with a greasy, glandular surface. Flowers are usually violet, pink, white or yellow on tall scapes.
genera.ecology: They grow in wet, nutrient-poor habitats: bogs, seeps, limestone cliffs and tropical cloud forest. Mexican species often grow on vertical rocks and have a pronounced dry season.

care.overview: Pinguicula care splits into three broad groups: Mexican, temperate and tropical. Getting the dormancy right is the key.
care.light: Bright light; Mexican species tolerate more sun than temperate ones.
care.water: Tray water with mineral-free water during growth; reduce or stop during dormancy.
care.soil: Peat : perlite : sand, or a mineral mix for Mexican species.
care.dormancy: Mexican species form succulent winter rosettes; temperate species die back to hibernacula; tropical species have no dormancy.
care.feeding: Self-catches small insects. Do not feed large prey or fertilise.
care.propagation: Leaf cuttings, division, seed.
care.problems: Rot, hard water, aphids, thrips, mealybugs.

mexican.label: Mexican
mexican.water: Wet during summer growth; almost dry during the winter succulent rosette.
mexican.soil: Equal parts peat, perlite and vermiculite, with a little sand; slightly alkaline is often used.
mexican.temperature: Warm days, cool nights; protect from frost.
mexican.dormancy: Dry winter dormancy with a small, succulent rosette.
mexican.notes: The classic Mexican butterworts. Keep dry in winter and resume watering when carnivorous leaves appear.

temperate.label: Temperate
temperate.water: Wet during growth; moist but not waterlogged in winter.
temperate.temperature: Cool to mild; winter cold required.
temperate.notes: Hardy bog butterworts for cool climates. They die back to a tight winter bud.

tropical.label: Tropical
tropical.notes: Warm, humid species from the Neotropics. Protect from cold and keep the air moving.

genera.nativeRange: North and South America, mainly Mexico and the south-western USA
genera.description: Proboscidea species are sticky-leaved annuals or short-lived perennials, famous for their woody seed pods with long, curved claws. The glandular leaves trap small insects but the plants are only weakly carnivorous. They are easy, fast-growing summer annuals.
genera.identification: Large, sticky, opposite leaves; tubular pink or purple flowers; long, hooked seed pods.
genera.ecology: Warm, dry, disturbed ground and desert washes. The claws help the seed pods attach to passing animals.

care.overview: An easy, fast annual for a warm sunny spot. Grow it for its strange seed pods as much as for its sticky leaves.
care.water: Moderate; drought-tolerant once established.
care.soil: Poor, sandy, free-draining soil.
care.dormancy: Annual.
care.feeding: No feeding.
care.propagation: Seed; soak and nick the hard coat.
care.problems: Aphids, spider mites, powdery mildew.

genera.nativeRange: Fynbos of the south-western Cape, South Africa
genera.description: Roridula is a South African shrub with long, sticky leaves that trap insects. Unusually, the plant does not digest its prey directly: a resident bug (Pameridea) feeds on the trapped insects and the plant absorbs nutrients from the bug's droppings. This delicate mutualism makes Roridula one of the most fascinating plants in the Cape flora.
genera.identification: A woody shrub with narrow, sticky leaves and small pink or white flowers. Look for the resident assassin bugs on the leaves.
genera.ecology: It grows in nutrient-poor fynbos on sandy soils. The plant depends on its resident bugs; plants without them can be nutrient-starved.

care.overview: A specialist Mediterranean shrub. It needs sandy, acidic soil, full sun, good airflow and its pollinating/resident insects for long-term health.
care.water: Keep moist during winter growth; reduce in summer but do not bake the roots.
care.soil: Very sandy, acidic peat mix with sharp drainage.
care.dormancy: Growth slows in the dry summer.
care.feeding: Do not feed the plant; it relies on trapped insects and resident bugs.
care.propagation: Seed (difficult) or cuttings.
care.problems: Root rot, low humidity, loss of resident insects, scale.

genera.nativeRange: Eastern and south-eastern North America, from Canada to Florida and Texas
genera.description: Sarracenia pitchers are tall, hollow leaves with a nectar-secreting rim, a slippery interior and downward-pointing hairs that guide insects to a digestive pool at the base. The genus includes the purple pitcher plant, the tall yellow trumpets and the hooded, nodding pitchers of Sarracenia psittacina. They are among the easiest and most rewarding carnivores for a sunny bog garden.
genera.identification: Hollow, tubular or hooded pitchers arising from a rhizome, with a wing along the front and a lid or hood. Flowers are large, nodding and bizarre.
genera.ecology: They grow in nutrient-poor pine savannas, bogs and seepages that depend on fire and clean water. Habitat loss and poaching have made several species rare.

care.overview: Full sun, wet feet and a cold winter dormancy. Perfect for an outdoor bog garden in a temperate climate.
care.light: Full sun; at least six hours of direct sun.
care.water: Stand in 2–10 cm of mineral-free water during growth. Keep the bog wet year-round.
care.soil: Peat : sand or perlite 1:1. Never use potting soil or fertiliser.
care.temperature: Temperate; most species are hardy with mulch or a sheltered bog.
care.dormancy: Cold winter dormancy is essential. Keep cool and moist, not warm and wet.
care.feeding: Outdoor plants catch their own insects. Do not fertilise.
care.propagation: Rhizome division in late winter; seed (slow).
care.problems: Rot in stagnant water, scale, aphids, squirrel and slug damage.

genera.nativeRange: Tropical West Africa: Sierra Leone, Liberia and Côte d'Ivoire
genera.description: Triphyophyllum peltatum is a remarkable tropical liana and one of the few plants known to be a facultative carnivore. In its juvenile phase it produces sticky, glandular leaves that trap insects; later it switches to ordinary leaves and a climbing habit. It is not a practical cultivated plant.
genera.identification: A large forest liana with three leaf types: glandular carnivorous leaves, ordinary leaves and hooked climbing leaves.
genera.ecology: It grows in tropical rainforest in West Africa. The carnivorous phase is thought to help the plant acquire nutrients during rapid early growth.

care.overview: Not recommended for cultivation. It needs tropical rainforest conditions and a large climbing structure.
care.water: High humidity and evenly moist, free-draining soil.
care.soil: Humus-rich tropical mix.
care.dormancy: None.
care.feeding: Not applicable in cultivation.
care.propagation: Seed or cuttings, with difficulty.
care.problems: Not a houseplant; leave wild plants undisturbed.

genera.nativeRange: Cosmopolitan, on every continent except Antarctica, with centres of diversity in South America and Australia
genera.description: Utricularia is the largest genus of carnivorous plants, with more than 240 accepted species. Its traps are tiny, hollow bladders that suck in water and prey when a trigger hair is touched, one of the fastest movements in the plant kingdom. Bladderworts grow as aquatics, terrestrials, epiphytes and even in wet sand.
genera.identification: Bladder-like traps on the stems, stolons or leaves; flowers are usually yellow, violet or white on tall scapes. Aquatic species may look like loose threads or floating mats.
genera.ecology: They occupy an extraordinary range of nutrient-poor wetlands, from acid bogs and lakes to wet cliffs and bromeliad tanks. Many are tiny and easily overlooked.

care.overview: The care group matters: aquatic, terrestrial or epiphytic. All want mineral-free water, bright light and a nutrient-poor mix.
care.water: Mineral-free water. Aquatics float or are anchored in shallow water; terrestrials stand in a tray.
care.soil: Aquatics need no soil; terrestrials use peat : sand : perlite; epiphytes use sphagnum or tree-fern fibre.
care.temperature: Depends on the species; most are warm-temperate to tropical.
care.dormancy: Aquatics may form turions; terrestrials may die back to a resting bud.
care.feeding: Do not feed; the traps capture microfauna.
care.propagation: Division, stolons, turions, seed.
care.problems: Algae, drying out, hard water, aphids and rot.

aquatic.label: Aquatic
aquatic.water: Soft, acidic water; keep the plants submerged or floating.
aquatic.soil: No soil; use a shallow tray or pond.
aquatic.notes: Grow in shallow, sunlit water with no fish. Winter turions form in cold conditions.

terrestrial.label: Terrestrial
terrestrial.water: Stand in 1–2 cm of mineral-free water.
terrestrial.notes: The easiest bladderworts. Many spread into a carpet and flower freely.

epiphytic.label: Epiphytic
epiphytic.water: High humidity; mist regularly and keep the mount moist.
epiphytic.notes: Tropical epiphytes for a terrarium or orchid house. Excellent airflow is essential.
